summary: This program stores four song titles in a PriorityQueue and then removes them one at a time with poll(), which always hands back the smallest remaining title in alphabetical order. It shows the difference between how a priority queue looks when you iterate over it and the order in which it actually serves its elements.

lines.text: PriorityQueue is the collection that keeps its elements ordered by priority rather than by insertion order, so it must be imported before it can be used.
The class name has to match the file name, so this code belongs in PlaylistApp.java.

lines.code: // Example: Playlist as a PriorityQueue (String titles only)
lines.text: The comments above this one are placeholders for the earlier exercises in the chapter; this section is the new work.

lines.code: PriorityQueue<String> titleQueue = new PriorityQueue<>(); // natural A–Z order
lines.text: With no Comparator passed to the constructor, the queue uses the natural ordering of String, which for text means alphabetical order.
offer() adds an element to the queue and lets it settle into position; the elements are deliberately added out of alphabetical order to prove the queue does the sorting.

lines.code: System.out.println("Initial queue contents (iteration order not guaranteed):");
lines.text: This warning matters: a PriorityQueue only promises that the head is the smallest element, not that a walk through the whole queue comes out sorted.
forEach with a method reference prints every element, and the jumbled result demonstrates the internal heap layout rather than a sorted list.
The loop keeps draining the queue until nothing is left, since poll() removes each element it returns.

lines.code: String nextTitle = titleQueue.poll(); // removes smallest (A–Z) first
lines.text: poll() takes the highest-priority element off the front, which here means the title that comes first alphabetically; repeating it yields the titles in full sorted order.
